title: The Tragedy of the Commons
summary: William Forster Lloyd noticed in 1833 that common pastures were more worn than private ones: each herder gains the whole benefit of adding an animal, but shares the cost of the damage with everyone. Garrett Hardin's 1968 essay made the idea famous. It was mainly about population growth, and it concluded that commons need privatising or "mutual coercion, mutually agreed upon". Critics pointed out that his pasture is open to anyone with no rules at all, which real commons rarely were, and Hardin later said he should have called it the tragedy of the unmanaged commons. Elinor Ostrom's fieldwork showed communities around the world managing shared resources for centuries by agreeing on their own rules, monitoring and sanctions.
citations: William Forster Lloyd, Two Lectures on the Checks to Population (Oxford, 1833)
